source.title: Smarter Saboteurs, Better Fixers: Scaling & Security in Linear Multi-Agent Workflows
source.authors: Tim Mcallister; Sina Abdidizaji; Ivan Garibay; Ozlem O. Garibay

record.tranche_reason: Applies model scaling to a new setting—linear multi-agent coding workflows under malicious-agent and correction conditions—and reports HumanEval performance. It does not test the original pretraining-loss or compute-allocation measurements.
record.gate_note: The study reports HumanEval Pass@1 across model sizes, prompting styles, and pipeline configurations. This bears on V6, downstream task performance versus scale, but it does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, training tokens or compute, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or find a compute-optimal allocation. The malicious condition is deliberately prompted and should not be read as ordinary model behavior. Cited scaling-law results are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: Its Control conditions report HumanEval Pass@1 for five sizes in each of two model families, which bears on V6. The paper is a multi-agent security study and fits no scaling function. The Malicious conditions induce sabotage on purpose, so they measure compliance with an adversarial prompt, not capability scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Larger models execute the malicious Engineer instruction more faithfully, so the drop grows with scale in No-Fix pipelines (up to 53.7pp). A terminal QA+Fixer stage restores statistical parity with Control at every size (no McNemar test significant after Holm correction). The authors call this a compliance–correction symmetry and argue that linear-topology brittleness reflects missing correction, not topology.
record.recipe_differences: Measures HumanEval Pass@1 in a multi-agent coding workflow rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy or compute-optimal model/data allocation; no power-law or extrapolation fit.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompting style changes results, especially for smaller models: native prompting can derail small models, while simplified prompting with prefix forcing improves task focus. The presence of terminal QA+Fixer also changes the malicious-condition outcome. The study reports both prompting styles, but the native QA+Fixer rows are omitted due to the row cap.

fits_no_version.finding: In uncorrected pipelines, the Control-minus-Malicious drop grows with size: for Qwen simplified, from 0pp at 0.8B to 53.7pp at 27B. A same-size QA+Fixer stage brings the drop to at most about 5pp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models execute deliberately induced sabotage instructions more faithfully (compliance scales with capability), and same-size correction stages scale comparably.

record.peer_reviewed: Published at the Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD) at ICML 2026.
record.problems: The results concern short algorithmic HumanEval tasks and a static, hand-curated malicious profile; tested models are at most 27B. All roles share a model instance. The malicious behavior is explicitly induced by the prompt. Pass@1 point estimates have no reported error bars; paired McNemar tests are reported for control-versus-malicious comparisons, with corrected significance described in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the 20 native-prompt QA+Fixer Pass@1 rows from Appendix A, Table 2, to stay within the 60-row limit. The retained rows include all simplified-prompt results from Table 1 and all native-prompt No-Fix results. The separately reported malicious-drop values are derived from the retained Control and Malicious Pass@1 values.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss, tokens or compute measured.
No fitted law and no extrapolation.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed size.
No other modality or training regime.

Predictability is not tested: no fitted curve against size, and pretraining loss is never used as a predictor. Sizes are released checkpoints, not a controlled training sweep, and the setting is a pipeline rather than the bare model.

record.verdict_notes: The relevance to scaling laws is incidental: the paper uses model size as an axis for a security study. Only the Control series bears on V6, and only on whether downstream performance rises with size, not on whether it does so predictably. Models are released Gemma 3 and Qwen 3.5 checkpoints (at most 27B), not a controlled training sweep. Qwen nears the HumanEval ceiling at 27B (97.56%). Kaplan et al. is cited only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and orders of magnitude.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.

No pretraining-loss predictor or fitted relationship is tested; the downstream measure is HumanEval Pass@1 in a specific linear multi-agent coding workflow, including deliberately malicious-agent conditions.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation are fitted or compared across fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Control pipelines: simplified prompting for both families, and native prompting for Qwen 3.5
relationships.reason: Control Pass@1 rises with size, e.g. Qwen simplified goes 23.17% to 97.56% and Gemma simplified 9.15% to 84.15%. The authors call the No-Fix Control rise monotonic. Rows s01,s03,s05,s07,s09,s11,s13,s15,s21,s23,s25,s27,s29,s31,s33,s35,s37,s39,n11,n13,n15,n17,n19.
relationships.display_finding: With simplified prompting, Pass@1 increased from 23.17% to 97.56% for Qwen and from 9.15% to 84.15% for Gemma, with monotonic improvement reported for No-Fix Control.

relationships.condition: Native MetaGPT prompting for small Gemma 3 models; Gemma 3 12B to 27B under simplified prompting
relationships.reason: Native Gemma 4B Control (30.49%) falls below 1B (36.59%) because of prompt-induced derailment, so the size trend depends on prompt choice. Gemma simplified plateaus from 12B to 27B (84.15% to 84.15%). Rows n03,n05,n07,n09,s13,s17,s19.
relationships.display_finding: Native prompting gave 4B only 30.49% versus 36.59% for 1B because of prompt-induced derailment, while simplified prompting left 12B and 27B tied at 84.15%.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Control pipelines across tested sizes, particularly simplified prompting; also the native Qwen 3.5 Control series
reader_labels.reason: HumanEval Pass@1 generally rises across model sizes in these benign settings; rows s01, s05, s09, s13, s17, s21, s25, s29, s33, s37, n11, n13, n15, n17, n19.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Malicious no-fix pipelines and native Gemma 3 small-scale prompting
reader_labels.reason: Under the deliberately malicious Engineer prompt, performance can be flat or substantially lower at larger sizes; native Gemma 3 Control also dips from 1B to 4B. The study itself attributes some small-model variation to prompting/derailment; rows s02, s06, s10, s14, s18, s22, s26, s30, s34, s38, n03, n05, n06.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Pass@1 in the malicious condition broadly tracks the Control series after terminal correction, with only small reported gaps in the matched results; rows s04, s08, s12, s16, s20, s24, s28, s32, s36, s40.
